note.text: A compound noun combines elements into a naming expression. It may be written as one word, with a hyphen or as separate words. The spelling is conventional, so check a learner’s dictionary rather than imposing one style on every compound. Many pluralise the last noun, but some mark a different head: mothers-in-law is a familiar example. Collocation concerns conventional combinations more broadly. A phrase can be natural without every combination being a compound noun.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to recognise a compound noun, choose a conventional form and preserve the relevant head in a plural. Builds on: word structure, nouns and natural combinations. Leads to: later formal writing and dictionary-based vocabulary extension.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original examples: notebook, bus stop and mother-in-law use different written styles. Their plurals need attention to the naming unit, not a rule that adds -s to the final letter of every expression. A learner takes notes and makes a decision; exchanging every verb with a synonym may spoil the collocation.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify what the compound names and consult its established spelling. Find the head when forming a plural. Keep spelling, word class and meaning distinct; a space does not stop an expression functioning as a compound noun. The lesson checks written recognition, not spoken stress.
